en: The various instructions of the Siddhas;
the various instructions of the Siddhas, [taught] by Padmāṅkura.

Wisdom and Means, having descended from the syllables Oṃ and Ha residing in the wheel of great bliss (mahāsukhacakra), are unified like a gem on a thread of knowledge; this is the instruction on Mahāmudrā by means of the swing.
[This is] of Prajñārakṣita.

The natural yoga (*sahajayoga*) consists of the swing (*dolā*), having made the thread of gnosis (*jñānatantu*) of equal flavor by entering the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), reaching the further shore of the reality of the instruction on the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) from the tip of the peak of the syllable-less, which is the true drop (*sadbindu*) experienced through the lotus and the vajra.
The drop of gnosis (*jñānabindu*), which is non-syllabic and rests upon the diamond-jewel at the *nelī* [the tip of the nose],
is declared by the wise Nelīpāda to be the bringer of swift accomplishment.
Ravigupta has declared:
"The form of the flame of the lamp of gnosis, situated between the emanation-lotus and the moon,
quickly melts the syllable *Haṃ*."
According to the Kṛṣṇācāryas:
"The Caṇḍālī, located in the center of the navel, is fully described by the Kṛṣṇācāryas;
having the nature of the primordial vowel (A), she burns from her mouth the Unstruck Sound (Anāhata)."
In the Nirmāṇa [kula], Tilaka is renowned; Vasanta resides in the Dharmacakra.
However, that both possess a single intrinsic nature was proclaimed by Kṛṣṇācārya.
Regarding the feet of Saraha:
"The visualization of the five syllables at the navel within the two nirmāṇacakra-s should be performed by one joined with yoga; this was proclaimed by Saraha."
In the *nirmāṇacakra* of Mahīdhara, Caṇḍālī, whose intrinsic nature is emptiness and who is fond of the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), is Mahīdhara.
Among those with many feet—
"In the pericarp of the excellent lotus at the *nirmāṇacakra* and other centers,
the letters *a* and *ha* become unified in the form of a lotus-fiber thread as the 'unstruck' (*anāhata*) and 'melting' (*drāvin*) sounds," so says Bhūripāda.
According to Vīṇāpāda:

In the *nirmāṇacakra*, [the two lines] arise from the *jñānabindu* within the union of the sun and moon; they are encircled three times by a line whose nature is the union of *āli* and *kāli*. Arising again, the two lines have the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of *prajñā* and *upāya*: one is white and, having returned from the *dharmacakra*, should be visualized; the second...
The Cakra, whose nature is wisdom, embraces the Anāhata as if it were a beloved; this is indeed the doctrine of Vīṇāpāda.
According to the teacher Virūpa:

"The wise one should count the syllable Oṃ situated in the space-cakra within the emanation-cakra by means of the mouth through the entry of the wind with the sound 'śīṭ'; thus it was taught by Virūpācārya.
The wise one should churn with the mouth until non-duality is attained."
The syllables *a* and *ha* were taught by Virūpācārya.
According to Nāgabuddhi:
the pericarp of the yoni-cakra situated within the emanation-lotus blazes and enters the dharma-cakra;
it becomes one with the line of the unstruck (*anāhata*) located at the site of the enjoyment [body]. This is the view of Nāgabuddhi.
Through the breath exiting and entering via the mouth of Diṅnāga,
one should churn the syllables *a* and *haṃ* until they attain non-duality; then, having placed it upon the lower tooth, one should press it with the tongue.
Diṅnāga says:
In the mouth of Mātali, there is the letter *ra* with a red mark (*aṃkāra*), and by means of the exiting breath.
And one should cause it to churn by means of the entry of the semen of skillful means (upāya) and the syllable *hūṃ*.
Through constant unification, Kakatuṇḍī becomes manifest;
the wise one should meditate on the drop of gnosis, resembling a pearl, at the tip of the nose.
Mātali declares that sounds reside within the ear.
Even the body, face, eyes, ears, and nose of Matsyendra— having attained [this state] through the restraint of the vital winds—
some hero blazes; such is the doctrine of Matsyendra.
In the *Uddeśasaṃuccaya*, it is said:

at the head of Prajñā is the syllable Oṃ; at the head of Upāya are two Hūṃs facing downward. In the center between them, within the opening of the Vajra and so forth, the Bindu, struck by the wind abiding in Prajñā, goes to the tip of the crest of Upāya. Struck by the wind of Upāya, the Bindu goes to the tip of the crest of [Prajñā]. The Jñānabindu, by virtue of its nature as bliss—

Being thus contemplated, [the seed-syllable] takes the form of the flame of the lamp of gnosis (*jñānadīpaśikhākāra*), embraced by the word *oṃ*. Being meditated upon as consisting of bliss, after the burning [of the fuel], from the flame there arises the meditation on that which consists of bliss. The *tilaka* is the syllable *oṃ*, and the spring season is the syllable *hūṃ*; they are of one nature, facing downwards, and not a mind consisting of bliss. In the two wheels (*cakradvaya*) are the syllables *lāṃ*, *hūṃ*, *mā*, and so forth, which cause the melting of the gnosis-bodhicitta (*jñānabodhicitta*). Thereafter, bliss—
It is mere cultivation.

Having turned back from the wheel and turned his face toward the *jñānabindu*, he gazes upon it; he embraces the beauty residing in the Wheel of Dharma and should cause the wind to enter through the vajra-face of the syllable Oṃ by way of its nature as bliss.

One should cause the syllable *oṃ*, emerging [from the mouth], to be drawn in by the wind and enter the syllable *hūṃ* mounted upon that wind; one should churn them until non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) is realized. One should place the tongue against the lower teeth, the row of teeth below. Non-substantiality is from the perspective of non-duality. By means of the "crow-beak" (*kākatuṇḍī*) [posture] of the wind—

The exit: it should emerge from the human nose. When the wind does not enter, one should make a sound in the form of a drop (*bindu*) that is pleasant to the ear, located at the tip of the nose, the tip of the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*), the tip of the mind, and the tip of the hollow of the throat.
From the very beginning, through meditation, one should press the mouth and other parts with the fingers of both hands; this is the meditation.
One should deliberate with excellence.
Thus ends the instruction of various Siddhas.
